IchiVaultOracle subsequently relies on this immutable dependency for base-token prices, so deployment with address(0), an EOA, or a nonresponsive implementation causes price queries to revert or fail permanently.
predictions.impact: The Ichi vault oracle can become unusable, causing supported-token checks, valuations, liquidations, and other operations depending on prices to revert or halt.
predictions.mitigation: Reject address(0) and require address(_base).code.length > 0 in the constructor. Validate that the supplied oracle returns a valid nonzero price for required base assets before registering the deployment.
predictions.title: Unvalidated Base Oracle Address Can Permanently Disable Pricing

predictions.description: WCurveGauge encodes only the gauge id and reward-per-share snapshot in each ERC1155 id. During burn it resolves the current gauge from gaugeController.gauges(gid) instead of preserving the gauge address used at mint time. If the controller mapping changes, existing positions are redeemed against a different gauge than the one holding the wrapper's deposited LP tokens.
predictions.impact: Users can be unable to redeem LP collateral and accrued rewards, potentially causing liquidation failures and permanent loss of access to positions until an external mapping restoration; a malicious replacement can also influence the token and withdrawal behavior used by redemption.
predictions.mitigation: Store the resolved gauge address or a mapping version in the position identity and redeem against that immutable value. Alternatively reject burns when the current controller mapping differs from the mapping recorded at mint and provide an explicit migration path.
predictions.title: Curve gauge remapping can strand or misroute existing wrapped positions

predictions.description: CoreOracle dispatches pricing to owner-configured route contracts without an on-chain validation that the route is an approved oracle, supports the requested token, or derives a trustworthy price. A compromised owner, governance misconfiguration, or malicious upgrade can therefore install an oracle that returns an attacker-selected price for collateral or debt assets.
predictions.impact: An attacker able to control the route authority can make collateral appear overvalued or debt appear undervalued, enabling undercollateralized borrowing or wrongful liquidation and potentially causing protocol-wide bad debt or loss of user collateral.
predictions.mitigation: Restrict route updates to a tightly governed authority and maintain an immutable or timelocked allowlist of approved oracle implementations and token-route pairs. Validate that each route is a contract, supports the configured token, returns a nonzero value within documented bounds, and preserves required decimals and freshness guarantees; emit events and provide delayed review for route changes.
predictions.title: Privileged route configuration can inject arbitrary asset prices

predictions.description: The adapter relies on feed-provided decimals when normalizing the signed answer to an 18-decimal price, but no bounded-decimal validation is documented. An improperly configured or nonstandard registry feed can return an excessively large decimals value, causing exponentiation or scaling to revert; high-decimal feeds can also produce materially rounded or zero prices.
predictions.impact: A malformed feed can make the Chainlink route revert and block borrowing, liquidation, or valuation operations; unsafe normalization can also produce incorrect collateral prices and cause undercollateralized positions or unfair liquidations.
predictions.mitigation: Validate feed decimals against an explicit supported range before exponentiation and normalize using checked arithmetic with separate branches for decimals above and below 18. Reject unsupported feeds or scaling results that overflow, underflow, or round to zero.
predictions.title: Unbounded Chainlink feed decimals can distort or disable price conversion

predictions.description: CurveSpell is marked as performing reward swaps with a zero minimum output. When harvested CRV or other gauge rewards are sold through the Uniswap V2 router without an effective amountOutMin bound, an attacker can front-run and back-run the swap, moving the pool price and forcing the spell to accept a severely unfavorable execution price.
predictions.impact: Harvested rewards can be exchanged for substantially less debt-repayment or collateral value than intended, causing direct losses to the leveraged position and potentially impairing solvency when the reward value is relied on to repay debt.
predictions.mitigation: Require a nonzero minimum output computed from a trusted quote with a bounded slippage tolerance, or use a protected execution mechanism such as a deadline plus validated oracle/TWAP pricing; reject swaps whose output is below the bound and ensure the bound cannot be attacker-controlled without validation.
predictions.title: CurveSpell reward swaps allow zero minimum output and are sandwichable

predictions.description: AuraSpell integrates directly with Uniswap for token conversions, but the available component context does not establish a nonzero minimum output or a bounded deadline for those swaps. If its swap parameters permit zero minimum output or an attacker-controlled path, a searcher can sandwich the transaction and force the spell to accept severely unfavorable execution.
predictions.impact: Reward or collateral tokens can be exchanged at a heavily manipulated rate, causing direct value loss for the position or reducing users' received proceeds.
predictions.mitigation: Require a nonzero, position-appropriate minimum output and a short user-specified deadline; validate swap paths and reject unsafe parameters before invoking Uniswap.
predictions.title: AuraSpell reward swaps may be executable with zero or caller-controlled slippage protection

predictions.description: ShortLongSpell delegates asset conversion to Paraswap, but the available component evidence does not show enforcement of a protocol-level minimum output, deadline, or route-price bound. A caller or a transaction manipulator can therefore cause the spell to execute a materially underpriced swap, including a zero-minimum route, while the resulting position or repayment accounting proceeds with the reduced output.
predictions.impact: Collateral or borrowed assets can be exchanged at a severe discount, reducing position value and potentially causing user losses, undercollateralized positions, or protocol bad debt.
predictions.mitigation: Require a caller-supplied minimum output that is checked against the actual Paraswap result, reject zero or otherwise unbounded minimums where appropriate, validate the source token, destination token, and input amount against the operation, and require a bounded deadline or equivalent freshness condition. Independently verify returned balances before finalizing position accounting.
predictions.title: ShortLongSpell Paraswap execution permits insufficient-output swaps

predictions.description: CurveOracle depends on a Curve address provider and registry rather than a self-contained, immutable registry implementation. If the configured address provider can be upgraded or otherwise returns a different registry, CurveOracle will trust the replacement registry's pool mappings and virtual-price responses without independently authenticating or validating them.
predictions.impact: Collateral LP tokens can be materially overvalued, allowing excessive borrowing, or undervalued, causing wrongful liquidations; a malicious registry can also make all Curve-backed price requests return arbitrary values or revert.
predictions.mitigation: Pin a vetted registry address at deployment where possible, or restrict and timelock any provider changes. Validate the resolved registry against an allowlist and verify expected code/interface behavior before accepting prices; add monitoring and emergency pause controls for registry changes.
predictions.title: Externally Mutable Curve Address Provider Can Replace the Trusted Registry

predictions.description: UniswapV2Oracle reads ERC20 decimals from both pool assets and uses decimal powers to normalize reserve-based prices. Without an explicit upper bound and checked normalization policy, a token reporting an excessively large decimals value can make 10**decimals overflow and revert, while inconsistent or nonstandard decimals can produce materially incorrect prices.
predictions.impact: A configured pair containing a nonstandard token can make oracle calls revert, disabling dependent protocol operations, or can cause collateral to be over- or undervalued and enable unsafe borrowing or liquidation decisions.
predictions.mitigation: Enforce a documented decimals range, avoid unchecked exponentiation, and fail closed for tokens whose metadata cannot be safely normalized.
predictions.title: Unbounded token decimals can break or distort Uniswap V2 price normalization

predictions.description: The relative-deviation calculation operates on uint256 oracle prices normalized to 1e18 and multiplies prices or price differences by 1e18 and a deviation factor without an evident upper-bound check. A sufficiently large externally returned price can overflow checked arithmetic and revert the deviation check, causing every dependent oracle query to fail.
predictions.impact: Oracle reads can revert, disabling collateral valuation, borrowing, liquidation, or other protocol operations that depend on the affected route.
predictions.mitigation: Validate that all input prices and the configured deviation are within safe bounds before arithmetic; calculate deviations using division-first or full-precision mulDiv logic, and reject values that cannot be represented safely.
predictions.title: BaseOracleExt deviation arithmetic can overflow and brick dependent price reads

ground_truth.description: USSDRebalancer.getSupplyProportion() uses the raw USSD/DAI token balances held by a Uniswap V3 pool to calculate the rebalance amount. In Uniswap V3, those balances need not correspond to the current pool price because they include accumulated fees and can reflect liquidity placed in different price ranges. Consequently, when USSD is below peg, USSDamount can be lower than DAIamount and the subtraction in rebalance() can revert. When USSD is above peg, an attacker can use high-range single-sided DAI liquidity to inflate DAIamount, causing rebalance() to mint and sell more USSD than required to restore the peg.
ground_truth.impact: Rebalancing can malfunction when the USSD/DAI balance proportion is not as expected. An attacker can manipulate that proportion so the protocol mints and sells more USSD than required to restore the peg. If the collateral asset is also manipulated, the protocol can trade at a manipulated price, causing greater damage to the protocol.
ground_truth.mitigation: Replace the pool-balance-based rebalance delta with a formula that accounts for the Uniswap V3 liquidity range when calculating the amount required to restore the peg.
ground_truth.title: H-9: Uniswap v3 pool token balance proportion does not necessarily correspond to the price, and it is easy to manipulate.

ground_truth.description: USSDRebalancer.getOwnValuation() reads sqrtPriceX96 from the Uniswap V3 DAI-USSD pool's slot0() and derives the USSD valuation from the instantaneous pool price instead of a time-weighted average price. A user can temporarily move this spot price by buying or selling assets, including with flash-loaned funds, and then call rebalance() using the manipulated valuation.
ground_truth.impact: The USSD price used by rebalance() can be manipulated within a transaction, allowing an attacker to trigger rebalancing with an attacker-controlled valuation.
ground_truth.mitigation: Use a TWAP price instead of the instantaneous slot0 price when calculating the USSD valuation.
ground_truth.title: H-5: Price calculation susceptible to flashloan exploits

predictions.description: rebalance() is publicly callable and bases both the trigger and trade size on uniPool.slot0() and ERC20 balances held by the pool. An attacker can temporarily manipulate the pool price or balances, invoke rebalance(), and cause the rebalancer to execute swaps using amountOutMinimum = 0, after which the attacker can restore the pool state or arbitrage the resulting trade.
predictions.impact: The rebalancer can sell USSD or collateral at an attacker-controlled price, causing direct loss of reserve assets and destabilizing the USSD peg.
predictions.mitigation: Use a sufficiently long TWAP or independently validated oracle for the trigger and sizing, validate pool liquidity/state, impose nonzero minimum outputs and deadlines, and restrict execution to an authorized keeper or enforce a commit/validation mechanism.
predictions.title: Permissionless rebalancing is manipulable through the Uniswap V3 spot price and pool balances

predictions.description: When ownval is below the lower threshold, rebalance() computes (USSDamount - DAIamount / 1e12) / 2 without checking that USSDamount is at least the normalized DAI amount. If the pool has more normalized DAI than USSD, Solidity 0.8 reverts before recovery can execute. The same function also evaluates 1e6 - threshold without validating threshold <= 1e6.
predictions.impact: Rebalancing becomes unavailable precisely during a depeg condition, preventing recovery and potentially leaving the pool exposed to prolonged insolvency or further arbitrage.
predictions.mitigation: Clamp trade sizes when the balance difference is negative, branch explicitly on the balance relation, and require threshold <= 1e6 in setTreshold before storing it.
predictions.title: Peg-down rebalance can revert from unsigned subtraction underflow

predictions.description: SellUSSDBuyCollateral intends to avoid swapping collateral tokens that are already the pool legs, but uses if (token != token0 || token != token1). For any token, at least one inequality is true, including when the token equals token0 or token1. The rebalancer can therefore execute pathbuy for a pool leg or base asset, potentially performing an unintended self/invalid swap or reverting during rebalancing.
predictions.impact: Rebalancing may revert or spend newly acquired base assets through an unintended route, causing denial of service or reserve loss.
predictions.mitigation: Replace the condition with token != uniPool.token0() && token != uniPool.token1(), validate every configured path against its input/output tokens, and skip or explicitly handle pool-leg collateral.
predictions.title: Collateral exclusion check is always true and can swap pool base assets incorrectly

predictions.description: USSD.mintRebalancer() and burnRebalancer() are public and do not apply the defined onlyBalancer modifier. Any account can mint arbitrary USSD to the USSD contract or burn any USSD currently held there, including tokens intended for rebalancing.
predictions.impact: An attacker can alter supply and collateralization accounting, force rebalancing decisions based on unauthorized supply changes, or destroy inventory accumulated for reserve operations, causing peg instability or denial of service.
predictions.mitigation: Apply onlyBalancer to both functions, or use an explicit role restricted to the configured rebalancer; reject zero or invalid rebalancer addresses during configuration.
predictions.title: Unrestricted mintRebalancer and burnRebalancer permit unauthorized supply manipulation

predictions.description: StableOracleWETH and StableOracleWBTC cast signed Chainlink prices directly to uint256 and ignore round completeness and timestamp freshness. A negative answer becomes a huge unsigned value, while stale data remains usable. StableOracleDAI initializes ethOracle to address(0), so any getPriceUSD call dereferences a zero address and reverts. Configured collateral using these feeds can therefore be mispriced or make minting, accounting, and rebalancing fail.

predictions.mitigation: Require price > 0, validate updatedAt and answeredInRound against the current round, enforce a maximum staleness bound, and inject and validate a nonzero ETH oracle before enabling the collateral.
predictions.title: Oracle implementations accept invalid or unavailable prices

predictions.description: The constructor permanently assigns the Ethereum-mainnet WETH/USD feed address 0x5f4eC3Df9cbd43714FE2740f5E3616155c5b8419 without checking chain ID, feed code, interface support, or deployment configuration. If this contract is deployed on another network, the address may be unset, unrelated, or expose incompatible data, causing getPriceUSD to revert or return an incorrect value that downstream minting and collateral valuation rely on.
predictions.impact: USSD minting and collateral valuation can be halted by oracle-call reverts or performed at a materially incorrect WETH price, potentially enabling undercollateralized issuance or loss of funds.
predictions.mitigation: Pass the intended feed address as a constructor parameter or select it from a chain-validated configuration; verify the target has contract code, supports AggregatorV3Interface, reports the expected asset pair and decimals, and reject deployment when the configured network/feed combination is invalid.
predictions.title: Network-specific hardcoded Chainlink feed can invalidate WETH pricing on non-mainnet deployments

predictions.description: The constructor initializes priceFeed with 0x5f4eC3Df9cbd43714FE2740f5E3616155c5b8419, which is the Chainlink ETH/USD feed, while the source comment identifies 0xf4030086522a5beea4988f8ca5b36dbc97bee88c as the intended BTC/USD feed. getPriceUSD therefore reports ETH's price as WBTC's price, and downstream oracle-priced minting and collateral calculations use the wrong asset valuation.
predictions.impact: WBTC-backed users may mint materially more or less USSD than their collateral warrants, enabling loss of protocol collateral or under-collateralized USSD issuance.
predictions.mitigation: Use the verified BTC/USD feed address for the target deployment, inject the feed address through a controlled constructor parameter, and validate that the configured feed's description, decimals, and network match BTC/USD before enabling the collateral.
predictions.title: StableOracleWBTC uses the ETH/USD Chainlink feed instead of BTC/USD

predictions.description: SimOracle.setPriceUSD is public and has no access control, so any account can overwrite the price consumed through getPriceUSD. If this oracle is configured for USSD collateral valuation, an attacker can set an artificially high price to mint excess USSD for little collateral or set a zero/low price to distort collateral factors and rebalancer trades.
predictions.impact: Unauthorized callers can cause undercollateralized USSD issuance, mispriced collateral-factor calculations, or unfavorable protocol trades, potentially resulting in direct loss of backing assets and insolvency.
predictions.mitigation: Restrict setPriceUSD to a narrowly authorized governance or test-only role, or remove this oracle from production deployments. Enforce nonzero and protocol-specific bounds, and use a time-delayed, auditable update mechanism where mutable simulation pricing is required.
predictions.title: Unrestricted SimOracle price setter allows arbitrary oracle-price manipulation

ground_truth.description: EUSDMiningIncentives.stakedLBRLpValue() values a user's staked WETH/LBR LP tokens from the pair contract's current WETH and LBR token balances. During a Uniswap V2 flash-swap callback, the transferred-out assets temporarily reduce those balances before the swap is repaid. An attacker can therefore understate a victim's LP value, make isOtherEarningsClaimable() return true, and call purchaseOtherEarnings() while the eligibility check is using the manipulated value.
ground_truth.impact: An attacker can redirect a victim's accumulated mining reward to themselves even though the victim has staked enough WETH/LBR LP tokens for the reward to remain protected from buyout.
ground_truth.mitigation: Use the WETH/LBR pair's recorded reserves returned by getReserves() instead of its live token balances when calculating the staked LP value.
ground_truth.title: [M-13] It is possible to manipulate WETH/LBR pair to claim reward of the users which shouldn't be claimed

predictions.description: GovernanceTimelock grants DAO to both the timelock itself and msg.sender in its constructor, while configurator functions protected by onlyRole(DAO) use checkOnlyRole and therefore accept the deployer directly without requiring timelock execution. The deployer can directly modify mint-vault activation, mint caps, token initialization and other DAO-controlled settings.
predictions.impact: A compromised or malicious deployer can enable arbitrary vaults, raise mint caps, alter core token configuration or change risk parameters, enabling unauthorized token inflation and protocol insolvency.
predictions.mitigation: Do not grant DAO to the deployment EOA, or revoke that grant after initialization. Ensure privileged configurator operations can only be executed by the timelock/governance executor and are subject to the intended delay.
predictions.title: Deployer retains direct DAO authority over critical configurator controls

predictions.description: distributeRewards transfers eUSD or PeUSD to ProtocolRewardsPool before calling notifyRewardAmount. notifyRewardAmount immediately returns when totalStaked() is zero, without recording the distribution or refunding the transferred tokens. Any distribution performed while the pool has no stake becomes unaccounted balance that cannot be allocated through the reward-per-token mechanism.
predictions.impact: Protocol-generated eUSD/PeUSD rewards can become permanently unclaimable, causing loss of rewards intended for future stakers and inaccurate reward accounting.
predictions.mitigation: Check totalStaked before transferring, or record pending rewards when there are no stakers and distribute them on the next valid notification. Verify transfer amounts and maintain explicit liabilities for undistributed rewards.
predictions.title: Protocol reward distributions are permanently stranded when no esLBR holders are staked

predictions.description: The earned() calculation applies getBoost(_account) to the entire rewardPerToken() delta since userUpdatedAt[_account]. Because the boost contract is queried only when the staking account is checkpointed and boost changes are not synchronized with the pool, a user can establish or increase a lock shortly before calling a pool function and have the higher boost applied to rewards accrued before the lock or boost change.
predictions.impact: The attacker can claim more LBR than the boost was active for, diluting other stakers and increasing minted reward supply beyond the intended allocation.
predictions.mitigation: Checkpoint staking rewards before any boost or lock status change, or calculate rewards over discrete intervals using historical boost state. Do not apply a newly observed boost to reward time preceding its activation.
predictions.title: Boosted rewards can be applied retroactively

predictions.description: setRewardsDuration() accepts any duration, including zero, and notifyRewardAmount() divides by duration without validating it. In addition, integer division in _amount / duration and (_amount + remainingRewards) / duration silently discards remainder tokens from each schedule.
predictions.impact: Reward scheduling can be made temporarily unavailable until governance repairs the duration, and users can receive fewer rewards than the amounts announced, with the cumulative shortfall retained outside the reward accounting.
predictions.mitigation: Require duration > 0 and enforce an appropriate minimum duration. Track and explicitly handle division remainders, or use fixed-point accounting so the full scheduled amount is either distributed or deliberately returned.
predictions.title: Reward duration accepts zero and reward scheduling truncates emissions

predictions.description: EUSDMiningIncentives.purchaseOtherEarnings obtains lbrPrice from latestRoundData and immediately casts it to uint256 and uses it in the buyout fee calculation. A zero answer makes the EUSD bidding fee zero, while a negative answer becomes a huge uint256 and can revert through arithmetic or token transfer. Stale or invalid rounds are also accepted.
predictions.impact: A zero-price feed can allow free acquisition of esLBR rewards; invalid or stale data can disable EUSD reward buyouts and disrupt reward operations.
predictions.mitigation: Require a positive answer, valid round metadata, and an acceptable updatedAt age before conversion. Define a bounded price sanity range and revert or disable the buyout when the feed is invalid.
predictions.title: LBR oracle result is used without zero, sign, or freshness validation during reward buyout

predictions.description: The stETH vault appears to account for deposited collateral using fixed raw stETH amounts while stETH balances are rebasing. A negative stETH rebase, such as one caused by validator losses or protocol slashing, reduces the vault’s actual token balance without reducing depositedAsset or totalDepositedAsset. Debt and collateral-ratio calculations can therefore continue treating the vault as fully collateralized even though less stETH is available for withdrawal or liquidation.
predictions.impact: The protocol can permit undercollateralized borrowing and incur bad debt after an adverse stETH rebase, with withdrawals and liquidations potentially exceeding the vault’s remaining stETH backing.
predictions.mitigation: Track stETH shares or compute each position’s current redeemable stETH amount using a rebasing-aware representation. Use the same current-value calculation for borrowing limits, collateral ratios, withdrawals, and liquidation, and add tests covering negative and positive rebases.
predictions.title: StETH rebasing can make recorded collateral exceed the vault’s actual collateral

ground_truth.description: Multipool.getSlots() reads each underlying Uniswap V3 pool's transaction-local slot0 price. _getReserves() feeds that price into LiquidityAmounts.getAmountsForLiquidity() to value the Multipool's positions, and deposit() uses the resulting reserves to optimize deposit amounts and calculate newly minted LP tokens. Because slot0 can be moved within a transaction, an attacker can distort the reserve ratio used for share issuance without changing the Multipool's durable economic value.
ground_truth.impact: A manipulated reserve calculation can cause deposits to mint an incorrect number of Multipool LP tokens, diluting other liquidity providers and causing them to receive fewer LP tokens or a smaller share of pool assets than intended.
ground_truth.mitigation: Use a manipulation-resistant TWAP or another independently validated price for reserve and share calculations instead of raw slot0. Reject deposits when each underlying pool's current price deviates beyond a configured bound from its weighted-average reference price.
ground_truth.title: H-3: Usage of `slot0` is extremely easy to manipulate

predictions.description: Multipool.getAmountOut always reads underlyingTrustedPools[500].poolAddress, regardless of the configured strategy or constructor fee list. Factory.createMultipool accepts arbitrary fee arrays, so a valid multipool created without fee 500 causes rebalanceAll to call observe on address(0) and revert.
predictions.impact: Liquidity cannot be rebalanced for affected pools, preventing strategy updates and potentially leaving assets in stale positions or blocking operational risk management.
predictions.mitigation: Use a configured trusted fee tier or a strategy-selected oracle pool, and validate oracle availability during pool creation and before rebalance. Reject zero-duration or unavailable observation configurations.
predictions.title: Rebalance is hardcoded to the 0.05% Uniswap pool and can be permanently unavailable

predictions.description: setParam casts the arbitrary _param value to uint32 for twapDuration without requiring it to be nonzero, within a practical observation window, or representable as a safe signed divisor. getAmountOut divides by int32(twapDuration) and requests that observation period from Uniswap V3.
predictions.impact: The operator cannot rebalance the pool, and an invalid configuration can make recovery require privileged administrative intervention.
predictions.mitigation: Require twapDuration > 0, <= type(int32).max, and within a documented maximum supported by the underlying pools; validate observation cardinality or handle unavailable history before allowing the parameter update.
predictions.title: Unbounded TWAP duration configuration can disable all rebalances

predictions.description: Multipool.deposit obtains slot data through getSlots, which reads each underlying Uniswap V3 pool's current slot0 price, and uses that data to calculate liquidity and LP issuance. Unlike the rebalance path, the deposit path has no demonstrated TWAP or manipulation-resistance check.
predictions.impact: The attacker may mint undervalued or overvalued LP tokens and redeem against reserves, transferring value from existing liquidity providers or causing unfair dilution.
predictions.mitigation: Use a sufficiently long and validated TWAP for deposit valuation, reject stale or insufficient observations, and enforce deposit minimums based on a manipulation-resistant reference price. Consider adding per-deposit price-impact limits and synchronizing valuation across all underlying positions.
predictions.title: Spot-price manipulation can distort deposit LP issuance

ground_truth.description: MavEthOracle.getPriceInEth() reads the current token reserves of a Maverick boosted position, multiplies them by externally sourced token prices, and divides by boosted-position total supply. A flash-loan-funded swap can move the Maverick pool, alter getReserves(), and raise or lower the oracle LP-token value before reversing the swap.
ground_truth.impact: Decreasing the oracle price can lower the totalDebt of LMPVault and let a user receive more LMPVault shares. Increasing the oracle price can raise the totalDebt of LMPVault and let a user receive more withdrawn tokens. Manipulating the oracle price can also cause protocol miscalculations in the Stats contracts.
ground_truth.mitigation: Replace the transaction-local reserve-sum valuation with a Maverick-specific fair-LP calculation that derives fair reserves from trusted component prices and the position's applicable invariant.
ground_truth.title: H-15: Maverick oracle can be manipulated

ground_truth.description: RdpxV2Core.bond() accepts a user-controlled bonding amount and, when reLP is active, passes that amount to ReLPContract.reLP(). The reLP operation then removes liquidity, swaps part of the removed WETH for rDPX, and adds liquidity again through Uniswap V2. Because the caller can control the size of this transaction-local liquidity operation through bond(), an attacker can manipulate the pool before bond() and profit from the resulting reLP sequence.
ground_truth.impact: An attacker can steal value from RdpxV2Core by crafting a profitable sandwich attack around bond() and its indirectly triggered reLP operation.
ground_truth.mitigation: Remove ReLPContract.reLP() from bond() and trigger it separately to prevent users from controlling the reLP operation indirectly.
ground_truth.title: [M-08] `reLPContract.reLP()` is susceptible to sandwich attack due to user control over `bond()`

predictions.description: The LP component is marked as having vault-only collateral updates, while option settlement transfers assets to the LP and the share value includes rDPX. If every asset-changing path does not synchronously invoke the authorized update, LP total collateral and per-share value can diverge from actual token balances. Deposits or withdrawals executed during that divergence can be priced against stale accounting.
predictions.impact: The attacker can acquire undervalued shares or redeem overvalued shares, causing direct loss of rDPX and other vault assets to honest LPs.
predictions.mitigation: Make balance-affecting operations and collateral-account updates atomic, derive managed assets from verified token balances where practical, and block deposits and withdrawals whenever the accounting state is stale or an update is pending.
predictions.title: Vault-only collateral updates can leave LP accounting stale across settlement and liquidity flows

predictions.description: The Uniswap V3 AMO is described as using a caller-set minimum output while returning swap tokens to the core. Even if only an administrator can initiate the swap, an attacker can observe the pending transaction and manipulate the pool price around execution when the supplied minimum is too permissive, causing the vault to receive materially less value.
predictions.impact: Vault liquidity can be exchanged for substantially fewer assets, reducing collateral backing and LP share value; repeated swaps can produce significant financial loss.
predictions.mitigation: Compute and enforce minimum output from a bounded oracle/TWAP quote and configured maximum slippage, require deadline and pool-parameter validation, and reject swaps whose realized price deviates beyond the protocol limit.
predictions.title: Caller-controlled Uniswap V3 minimum output exposes vault swaps to adverse execution

ground_truth.description: MagicLpAggregator.latestAnswer() calculates the MagicLP token price from pool reserves. Because those reserve values can be manipulated, an attacker can use a flash loan to inflate the MagicLP oracle price.
ground_truth.impact: A flash-loan-funded swap can substantially inflate the MagicLP oracle valuation within one transaction.
ground_truth.mitigation: Before using pool reserves, compare the pool's base/quote price with the Chainlink-derived base/quote price and revert when the deviation exceeds a defined limit.
ground_truth.title: [H-04] Oracle price can be manipulated

predictions.description: updateExchangeRate() falls back to the previously cached exchangeRate whenever oracle.get() reports updated=false. Borrowing and the solvent modifier then use that stale rate for collateralization checks. If the collateral price falls while the oracle is unavailable or returns an unsuccessful update, borrowers can remain classified as solvent and borrow additional MIM against insufficient collateral; liquidators may also be unable to liquidate those positions until the oracle recovers.
predictions.impact: Cauldron reserves can incur bad debt because borrowers can extract MIM against collateral whose current value is materially below the cached valuation; liquidation protection can remain ineffective during the oracle outage.
predictions.mitigation: Track the timestamp or validity window of the cached rate and reject new borrowing or other risk-increasing operations when the rate is stale. Alternatively, use a conservative fallback valuation and preserve liquidation availability without allowing additional debt under an invalid price.
predictions.title: Stale oracle price is trusted during oracle failure, enabling undercollateralized borrowing

predictions.description: MagicLpAggregator.latestAnswer casts oracle.latestAnswer() values to uint256 without checking that they are positive, scales them and the reserves without overflow guards beyond Solidity reverts, and divides by pair.totalSupply() without checking for zero. A negative feed answer, zero-supply pool, zero-decimal mismatch, or excessive values can make the aggregator revert whenever the Cauldron queries the oracle.
predictions.impact: Oracle updates can revert and prevent borrowing, liquidation, and other risk-management operations for the affected Cauldron, potentially trapping collateral and allowing bad debt to persist.
predictions.mitigation: Require positive and fresh underlying answers, validate decimals and bounded magnitudes, reject zero totalSupply before division, use checked intermediate bounds, and define a non-reverting fallback or emergency oracle path for invalid pool/feed states.
predictions.title: Malformed MagicLP aggregator responses can permanently block oracle-dependent Cauldron operations

predictions.description: CauldronV4.updateExchangeRate stores any rate returned with updated=true, including zero, without validating that the rate is nonzero or within configured bounds. In _isSolvent, the debt-side value is multiplied by _exchangeRate, so a zero rate makes every account with collateral appear solvent regardless of its borrow part.
predictions.impact: Borrowers can create effectively uncollateralized MIM debt while solvency checks and liquidation eligibility are incorrectly bypassed, producing protocol bad debt.
predictions.mitigation: Reject zero and out-of-range rates, validate the oracle response before updating storage, and retain the last known-good rate or enter a fail-closed mode when sanity checks fail.
predictions.title: Cauldron accepts a zero exchange rate from a successful oracle update

predictions.description: The contract accepts an arbitrary staking token and the staking path is shown to use the requested amount as the stake amount. If the token charges transfer fees, rebases downward, or otherwise delivers fewer tokens than requested, the contract can record more staking principal than it actually receives. Later withdrawals may revert due to insufficient balance or leave the final stakers unable to recover their principal.
predictions.impact: The staking pool can become insolvent for later withdrawals, causing withdrawal denial or loss of users' deposited tokens.
predictions.mitigation: Either restrict stakingToken to known non-rebasing, non-fee-on-transfer tokens or calculate the received amount from pre- and post-transfer balances and use that actual amount consistently in total-supply, user-balance, and withdrawal accounting.
predictions.title: Fee-on-transfer staking tokens can make internal principal accounting exceed actual holdings

predictions.description: Reward tokens are configurable by the owner and the contract distributes multiple arbitrary ERC20 reward tokens. If notifyRewardAmount records the requested reward amount while the transfer into the contract delivers less because of transfer fees, the global reward rate and reward-per-token accounting can promise more tokens than the contract holds. Reward claims will then revert or become underfunded.
predictions.impact: Reward claims can fail for some or all users, and accrued rewards can become permanently uncollectible or cause distribution insolvency.
predictions.mitigation: Measure the reward-token balance delta when funding and calculate the reward schedule from the actual received amount; alternatively reject fee-on-transfer and rebasing reward tokens during configuration.
predictions.title: Fee-on-transfer reward tokens can create unpayable reward liabilities

predictions.description: BlastDapp unconditionally calls configurePointsOperator on the fixed Blast Points address during construction. On any chain or fork where that address has no compatible contract, the external call reverts and the entire deployment fails. If deployment tooling permits an incorrect chain or a supported network changes the endpoint, this creates a deployment denial of service.
predictions.impact: BlastDapp and any deployment depending on it cannot be deployed on the affected network, potentially blocking protocol rollout or upgrades.
predictions.mitigation: Restrict deployment to the intended Blast chain, validate the chain ID and target code before calling, and make the points endpoint an immutable constructor parameter selected from a deployment-time allowlist. If points configuration is optional, separate it from construction and handle failure explicitly.
predictions.title: Hardcoded Blast Points endpoint can make deployments fail outside Blast

predictions.description: MasterContractManager’s whitelist controls whether a master contract may be registered, but DegenBox authorization is based on the stored masterContractOf mapping and user approval. If whitelistMasterContract is later set to false, existing users remain associated with that master contract and their approvals remain effective because the authorization path does not appear to re-check the current whitelist status.
predictions.impact: Emergency removal of a malicious or compromised master contract can fail, allowing unauthorized withdrawals or transfers of approved users’ DegenBox assets until every user individually revokes or removes the association.
predictions.mitigation: Make DegenBox authorization require that the associated master contract remains currently whitelisted, or maintain a per-master-contract revocation epoch checked by DegenBox. Provide an owner-controlled mechanism to invalidate existing associations and approvals when a master contract is disabled.
predictions.title: Whitelisting revocation does not disable existing master-contract associations

ground_truth.description: V3Oracle.getValue() computes position token amounts from the current Uniswap V3 slot0() price and values them using oracle-derived token prices. _checkPoolPrice() bounds the current pool price against the oracle-implied pool price through maxPoolPriceDifference, but an overly permissive setting can still materially distort the valuation of tight-range positions.
ground_truth.impact: With a tight-range position and a fringe or incorrect maxPoolPriceDifference configuration, an attacker can cause non-dust collateral misvaluation and borrow against an overstated position value. The check limits the effect for wide-range positions and properly constrained configurations; repay() is unaffected because it does not use the oracle.
ground_truth.mitigation: Calculate amount0 and amount1 from the oracle-derived price rather than the current pool spot price returned by slot0().
ground_truth.title: [M-19] `V3Oracle` susceptible to price manipulation

predictions.description: FlashloanLiquidator.uniswapV3FlashCallback is an externally callable callback that decodes caller-supplied data and performs vault liquidation and swaps. The architecture does not indicate validation that msg.sender is the configured Uniswap V3 pool or that the callback belongs to an active liquidation initiated by liquidate. If either check is absent, an attacker can invoke the callback directly with crafted amounts and liquidation parameters.
predictions.impact: Unauthorized liquidation execution and arbitrary swap activity could be triggered; depending on repayment and balance handling, attacker-controlled calls may steal liquidator-held tokens or cause loss of vault/liquidation funds.
predictions.mitigation: Require msg.sender to equal the configured flash-loan pool, validate factory/pool provenance where applicable, and bind the callback to an operation-specific pending state containing the expected pool, tokens, amounts, and liquidation target; clear that state after completion.
predictions.title: Flash callback may accept forged callbacks without pool and operation authentication

predictions.description: AutoCompound performs pool swaps with a TWAP check, but a TWAP bound alone does not establish a user-specific minimum output, maximum input, deadline, or price-impact limit. An attacker can sandwich the transaction or move the pool price within the permitted TWAP deviation, causing the compound swap to execute at an unfavorable rate while still passing validation.
predictions.impact: Compounded fees or collateral can be exchanged below fair value, transferring value to the attacker and reducing users' position value.
predictions.mitigation: Require caller-supplied or owner-configured minimum output and maximum input values, enforce a short deadline and maximum price impact, and validate the final execution price against both TWAP and transaction-specific slippage limits.
predictions.title: TWAP-bound pool swaps may still permit economically harmful execution within the accepted deviation

predictions.description: AutoExit is described as allowing an NFT owner to configure a position while a separate operator executes it. If configuration is stored by NFT/token ID and is not cleared or revalidated when ownership transfers, a former owner can configure an exit recipient or parameters, transfer the NFT, and leave the new owner exposed to an operator-triggered exit using stale authorization or payout data.
predictions.impact: The current NFT owner may lose control of the position and proceeds may be redirected to a former owner or another configured recipient.
predictions.mitigation: At execution time, resolve and verify the current NFT owner and bind configuration to the current owner rather than only the token ID. Clear or invalidate configurations on NFT transfer, and require the current owner to reauthorize any payout recipient or exit parameters.
predictions.title: AutoExit configuration may remain bound to a token ID after NFT ownership changes

predictions.description: If share conversion counts outstanding loans as assets but withdraw and redeem attempt to transfer only immediately available tokens, a holder may receive a valid-looking maxWithdraw or redeem quote that reverts because assets are illiquid. An attacker can force or amplify this condition by borrowing available liquidity or creating positions that leave the vault underfunded.
predictions.impact: Lenders can be unable to withdraw or redeem during stressed conditions, creating a denial of service and potentially trapping funds while debt resolution occurs.
predictions.mitigation: Base maxWithdraw and maxRedeem on transferable cash after reserves, or implement an explicit withdrawal queue/claim mechanism; ensure preview functions and actual withdrawal paths use consistent liquidity-aware accounting.
predictions.title: ERC-4626 redemption can overstate liquidity when assets are lent out

ground_truth.description: WooPPV2 enforces maxNotionalSwap and maxGamma independently for each swap, then writes the swap's newPrice back to WooracleV2_2. A later swap in the same transaction reads that already-moved price as its starting state. Consequently, an attacker can split a flash-loaned WOO sale into multiple individually permitted swaps, compound the WOO price downward, and then sell a small amount of quote token at the manipulated price to receive more WOO than was borrowed. For a token without a configured Chainlink reference, WooracleV2_2 treats the nonzero internal price as in-bound, so the feasibility check does not provide an independent anchor.
ground_truth.impact: An attacker can extract the pool's base-token reserves and repay the flash loan from the proceeds, retaining the excess tokens as profit.
ground_truth.mitigation: Explicitly declare that tokens without a Chainlink price feed are not supported.
ground_truth.title: H-1: Pool can be drained

predictions.description: WooracleV2 stores one global timestamp and isWoFeasible(base) checks that timestamp for every asset. Any authorized update to one asset refreshes feasibility for all assets, including assets whose prices have not been updated. Consequently, WooPPV2 can continue pricing swaps with stale prices for otherwise inactive tokens.
predictions.impact: Users or liquidity providers can suffer losses from swaps executed at stale prices, potentially draining the pool's reserves of an affected token.
predictions.mitigation: Store a last-update timestamp per base token and validate that timestamp in isWoFeasible. Ensure every price, spread, and coefficient update updates only the relevant token timestamp, and use the per-token timestamp in all pool feasibility checks.
predictions.title: Global oracle timestamp allows stale asset prices to remain feasible

predictions.description: The native-input branch only requires fromAmount <= msg.value, but wraps the entire msg.value and transfers only fromAmount to WooPP. Any excess value is left as WETH in WooRouterV3 rather than refunded to the caller, allowing accidental overpayment to become stranded and potentially recoverable only through privileged recovery functionality.
predictions.impact: Users can permanently lose the excess native currency sent with a swap; accumulated surplus WETH may remain inaccessible or depend on an administrative recovery path.
predictions.mitigation: Wrap and transfer exactly fromAmount, or explicitly refund msg.value - fromAmount to the caller after the swap while safely handling failed ETH transfers.
predictions.title: WooRouterV3 retains excess native currency as stranded WETH

predictions.description: The WooCrossFee constructor assigns _wooracle, _wooPP, and _helper directly without rejecting zero addresses or verifying that the configured contracts implement the expected behavior. A deployment with an invalid or malicious dependency can make currentBalance or fee calculations revert, return attacker-controlled values, or otherwise produce incorrect cross-chain fees. Because these references are initialized only in the constructor, recovery may require redeployment if no trusted setter exists.
predictions.impact: Cross-chain transfers can be blocked by repeated quote reverts, or users can be charged incorrect fees and protocol accounting can be distorted by attacker-controlled balance or oracle responses.
predictions.mitigation: Reject zero addresses during construction and validate that each dependency supports the expected interface and trusted implementation. Use controlled setters with event emission, access control, and validation if dependency replacement is required; otherwise make the references immutable after verified initialization.
predictions.title: Unvalidated external dependency addresses can permanently disable or corrupt fee quoting

ground_truth.description: PanopticFactory._mintFullRange() reads the Uniswap V3 pool's instantaneous sqrt price from slot0() and uses it to calculate the full-range liquidity minted during deployNewPool(). Because the factory does not validate this price against an oracle or a time-weighted average, an attacker can manipulate the spot price with flash-loaned funds before deployment and cause a highly inaccurate liquidity calculation.
ground_truth.impact: The manipulated spot price can cause the factory to mint an inaccurate amount of liquidity for each token, resulting in an unbalanced newly deployed pool.
ground_truth.mitigation: Consider using the TWAP price instead of the spot price.
ground_truth.title: [M-01] `PanopticFactory` uses spot price when deploying new pools, resulting in liquidity manipulation when minting

predictions.description: uniswapV3MintCallback validates only that msg.sender is a canonical Uniswap pool and then transfers the callback-specified amounts from the arbitrary payer encoded in data. It does not verify that the callback corresponds to an SFPM-initiated mint or that a mint context is active. An attacker can call a canonical pool's mint function directly with recipient set to SFPM and callback data naming a victim as payer, causing SFPM to pull any tokens the victim has approved to SFPM. The resulting liquidity is owned by SFPM rather than the victim or attacker and cannot be recovered through the normal SFPM position interface.
predictions.impact: A victim with an SFPM token approval can be forced to transfer tokens into Uniswap liquidity that is not represented by a recoverable SFPM position, causing direct loss or permanent locking of funds and enabling approval-based griefing.
predictions.mitigation: Track an active mint context containing the expected pool, payer, and relevant operation data before calling Uniswap, and require the callback to match that context. Alternatively require the callback payer to equal the original SFPM caller and reject callbacks when no SFPM mint operation is active; clear the context after completion.
predictions.title: Uniswap mint callback can be triggered through an unsolicited direct pool mint

predictions.description: DonorNFT authorizes issuance solely by comparing msg.sender with the mutable panopticFactory address. The owner can replace this address at any time, including with an attacker-controlled contract or the zero address. A malicious replacement can call issueNFT repeatedly for arbitrary recipients, while setting the address to zero causes all legitimate factory issuance calls to revert.
predictions.impact: An attacker can counterfeit donor rewards and corrupt NFT ownership/accounting, and can permanently interrupt legitimate donor reward issuance until the owner repairs the configuration.
predictions.mitigation: Set the factory immutably during construction or restrict changes to a controlled governance process with a timelock and event emission. Reject address(0), validate that the replacement is the canonical PanopticFactory, and consider a one-time initialization guard if factory replacement is not required.
predictions.title: Owner-controlled factory can arbitrarily mint donor NFTs or permanently disable issuance

predictions.description: The four approve calls discard their return values. ERC20 tokens are permitted to return false without reverting, so initialization can appear successful while SFPM or a CollateralTracker has no usable allowance. Subsequent liquidity, collateral, or withdrawal operations then fail.
predictions.impact: The affected pool can be permanently unable to mint positions, move collateral, or perform other token transfers, locking or disabling associated protocol functionality.
predictions.mitigation: Use a safe approval helper that requires a successful return value or accepts no-return tokens according to a documented compatibility policy, and revert initialization when the required allowance is not established.
predictions.title: Ignored approve return values can leave pools initialized with unusable allowances

predictions.description: computeName and computeSymbol concatenate arbitrary strings returned by external token symbol() calls. The try/catch handles reverts but does not impose a length limit on successful dynamic return data. A malicious or pathological ERC20 can return an extremely large symbol, causing excessive memory expansion or gas consumption during metadata construction and potentially reverting pool or collateral initialization.
predictions.impact: Pool or collateral deployment/initialization, or metadata-dependent calls, can run out of gas or revert, preventing creation or use of the affected market.
predictions.mitigation: Bound the maximum returned symbol length before concatenation, use a bounded metadata read, or replace oversized/malformed values with a fixed placeholder.
predictions.title: Unbounded token metadata can cause gas or memory denial of service

predictions.description: FeesCalc reads Uniswap fee-growth accumulators as unsigned values, computes fees, and packs the result into signed LeftRight values. If the calculated fee exceeds the representable signed component range, an unchecked or narrowing conversion can truncate or reinterpret the value instead of rejecting it. The resulting negative or corrupted fee can be consumed by PanopticPool accounting.
predictions.impact: Position fee accounting can become corrupted, potentially allowing incorrect withdrawals, undercharging of owed fees, or denial of service if downstream arithmetic reverts on the corrupted value.
predictions.mitigation: Validate each computed fee against the exact int128/component bounds before packing; reject out-of-range values. Preserve Uniswap's intended modulo arithmetic for accumulator deltas separately from the bounded conversion, and add tests for accumulator wraparound and maximum representable fee values.
predictions.title: Uniswap fee-growth values can overflow signed fee packing

predictions.description: The transfer helpers rely on the low-level call succeeding and on permissive return-data checks, but do not verify that the token address contains contract code. Calls to an EOA or destroyed contract can therefore succeed without moving any tokens. If a pool or collateral flow is initialized with such an address, mint or callback accounting can proceed as though payment occurred.
predictions.impact: Positions or liquidity can be credited without receiving underlying assets, causing pool insolvency and enabling unauthorized withdrawals or losses for depositors and liquidity providers.
predictions.mitigation: Require the token address to contain contract code before transfer operations, and validate token code and ERC20 behavior when registering or initializing pools. Where possible, verify post-transfer balance changes instead of relying solely on low-level call success.
predictions.title: SafeTransferLib silently accepts transfers to non-contract token addresses

ground_truth.description: PanopticPool.pokeOracle() is permissionless and passes the current Uniswap pool tick to RiskEngine.computeInternalMedian(). OraclePack.computeInternalMedian() records the observation only when the current epoch differs from the recorded epoch. An attacker can manipulate the pool's current tick before an update, cause that value to be clamped and inserted into the internal oracle, and prevent later calls in the same epoch from replacing it. Repeating this across epochs can progressively move the oracle away from the legitimate market price.
ground_truth.impact: Manipulating the internal oracle causes positions to be evaluated at incorrect prices, which can produce incorrect solvency validations, unfair liquidations, or allow insolvent positions to remain active.
ground_truth.mitigation: Update the oracle continuously with the current tick as time progresses, similar to a Uniswap TWAP, instead of allowing only one update per epoch. Alternatively, restrict pokeOracle() to trusted callers or use a commit-reveal scheme to prevent frontrunning.
ground_truth.title: [M-11] An attacker can manipulate oracle easily

predictions.description: PanopticFactoryV4 is observed to require only a nonzero risk-engine address before deploying a pool. Without validating that the address is an approved implementation or otherwise enforcing the expected RiskEngine behavior, a caller able to select this parameter can deploy a pool backed by a malicious contract that returns permissive collateral and solvency assessments.
predictions.impact: The malicious pool can accept undercollateralized positions and permit withdrawals or trades that should fail, potentially causing deposited collateral to be lost when the pool becomes insolvent.
predictions.mitigation: Restrict pool creation to an approved risk-engine registry or bind the factory to an immutable trusted implementation; verify code/interface compatibility and prevent arbitrary risk-engine addresses from being registered for production pools.
predictions.title: Factory accepts an unauthenticated risk-engine address
